originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site at slug learn-verify-agent-output, for a reader who is already shipping agent output but has no reliable way to know when to trust it. Terminal task: build a three-layer verification gate for their own real project and use it to overturn one agent 'done' claim. Six lessons on the mechanism behind premature completion claims, why unit tests passing is not task completion, externalising the termination decision, layered verification, actionable failure feedback the agent can act on, and wiring the gate into a real project. The course competes head-on with a 13.7k-star repository whose lecture on this topic cites Guo et al. 2017 (ICML, neural-network calibration on image classifiers) to argue that 2026 coding agents overclaim completion; that argument must not be reproduced, and the overclaiming mechanism must be grounded in first-party observations of coding agents on real multi-step tasks or in peer-reviewed work on agents specifically.
learnerBrief: The reader runs agents on real multi-step work in a repository they own, and ships or nearly ships the result. They can run a command and edit a file; they are not assumed to know any particular test framework, CI system, or harness configuration format. Their problem is not that they trust agent output too much — they already distrust it — but that distrust has not turned into a repeatable check, so verification happens on the runs where they are already suspicious and gets skipped on the rest. They need a gate cheap enough to survive daily use, whose verdict does not depend on them reading a transcript.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request specified the target reader ('already shipping agent output, but has no reliable way to know when to trust it'), the terminal task (build a three-layer verification gate for their own real project and use it to overturn one agent 'done' claim), the lesson count and six themes, the concept ceiling, the differentiation requirement against a named competitor including the specific flawed argument to avoid, an explicit prerequisite boundary against learn-agent-first-real-task lesson 4 (which teaches reading an agent's actions by hand, so this course must teach gates that do NOT depend on a human reading the transcript), and a specific source-verification task on the Sonar survey figure. Starting point, goal, and constraints were all supplied; no clarification was needed.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer who already delegates multi-step work to a coding agent in a repository they own, ships the result, and has no repeatable way to distinguish a finished task from a confident summary.
knownConcepts: Running an agent on a multi-step task and reading its final summary
Running commands in a terminal from a repository root
Editing files in a repository and using version control
That automated tests exist and that a suite can pass or fail
Reading JSON well enough to edit a value in a structured file
unknownConcepts: Any specific test framework's API or configuration syntax
CI provider configuration (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or equivalent)
Browser automation tooling — Playwright, Puppeteer, or MCP server setup
Harness hook configuration formats and lifecycle event names
Writing the underlying unit tests for a feature
Multi-agent orchestration or agent SDK programming
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: The learner's own repository, terminal, and editor, with an agent they already use. No embedded sandbox, no specific language or framework, no CI account, and no browser automation installed. Lesson 6's gate script is shown in bash with npm commands as one concrete instance and states that any command producing an exit code substitutes; the hook mechanism is taught as a lifecycle event that can refuse a completion, with the explicit warning that event names and JSON shapes are product surface that changes between versions.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: After Lesson 1, take the final message from one of their own recent agent runs and sort every sentence into reported beliefs versus external signals, then check one reported belief by hand against the repository. This needs only reading a message they already have and running one command or opening one file — both in knownConcepts.
noviceRamp: The first two lessons require no new tooling at all: the reader works on completion messages they already have and on a test suite they already run, so the diagnosis lands before anything must be built.

Every technical term is introduced by an everyday handle first, then a visible instance, then the formal name: 'the list of what finished means' precedes done-condition; 'a change that passes the tests' precedes plausible patch; 'a lifecycle event that can refuse a completion' precedes Stop hook.

The gate is built one layer per stage rather than all at once — Lesson 3 produces a conditions file with no automation, Lesson 4 orders checks the reader already runs, Lesson 5 rewrites message text, and only Lesson 6 wires a trigger.

Lesson 6's exercises accept a partial gate: a layer 3 consisting of starting the app and performing one request is stated as an honest minimum, so a reader with no browser automation still completes the terminal task.

Every command in Lesson 6 states where it runs (the repository root), what success looks like (exit 0 and a GATE PASS line), and how to confirm the trigger fires (deliberately break a condition and watch for red without invoking the gate).

scope: Covers where a completion claim comes from and why self-review does not check it; what a passing test suite leaves unmeasured, with the measured gap between an automated grader and maintainer acceptance on agent-written patches; writing a done-condition that lives outside the agent's judgment and resists being edited to pass; ordering checks into three layers by cost so the cheapest fails first; writing failure output an agent can act on without human translation; and installing the gate on a trigger the reader does not control. Deliberately excludes: writing the underlying unit tests, choosing or configuring a CI provider, browser automation setup, evaluating models against benchmarks, and reading an agent's action trail by hand — the last belongs to learn-agent-first-real-task lesson 4, and this course deliberately teaches gates whose verdict does not depend on a human reading the transcript.

evidence: METR, 'Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main', published 2026-03-10: 4 maintainers from 3 repositories reviewed 296 AI-generated PRs, finding the automated grader about 24.2 percentage points higher than the maintainer merge decision, normalised against a 68% golden baseline. Fetched and read in full 2026-08-23.

Anthropic, 'Harness design for long-running application development', published 2026-03-24: first-party observation that agents asked to evaluate their own work respond by confidently praising it, and that separating the working agent from the judging agent is a strong but incomplete lever. Fetched and read in full 2026-08-23.

Anthropic, 'Effective harnesses for long-running agents', published 2025-11-26: first-party observation of the survey-and-conclude pattern and of unit tests and curl checks passing while a feature did not work end-to-end. Fetched and read in full 2026-08-23.

Sonar, '2026 State of Code Developer Survey report', fieldwork October 2025, published 2026-01-08: primary PDF retrieved and text-extracted 2026-08-23, confirming n=1,149, the exact wording of the 96% and 48% figures, and that the 96% is the residual of an agreement scale in which 4% completely agreed.
ImpossibleBench (arXiv 2510.20270, submitted 2025-10-23): cheating-rate methodology and the measured effect of read-only test access, full text read 2026-08-23.

Claude Code hooks reference at code.claude.com, fetched as raw markdown 2026-08-23: Stop event semantics, the block decision and required reason, the 8-consecutive-block override, and the documented rule that a silent hook does not approve.
topicCurrency.staleRisk: Highest risk is Lesson 6's hook material (S9): hook event names, JSON field names, decision schemas, and the 8-consecutive-block bound are product surface and change between Claude Code versions — the lesson carries an explicit in-prose warning to read current documentation and treat the mechanism rather than the syntax as durable. Second, all model names in the evidence (Claude 3.5 Sonnet through 4.5 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4.1, GPT-5) date the measurements; METR states its newest model is Claude Sonnet 4.5 and that newer models may differ, and the course repeats this. Third, ImpossibleBench's cheating rates are prompt-sensitive by a factor the paper itself measured (above 85% to 1% across prompt wordings), so they will not reproduce under different scaffolds. Fourth, the METR rejection-reason profile shifted between model generations within the study itself, so the claim that code quality dominates over broken functionality is the most likely finding to invert. Fifth, Sonar's survey is annual; the 2027 edition will supersede these figures. Sixth, the npm/bash commands in Lesson 6's gate script are one concrete instance and will not match a non-JavaScript project.
topicCurrency.competitorDifferentiation: The 13.7k-star walkinglabs/learn-harness-engineering lecture 9 ('Preventing Agents from Declaring Victory Too Early', read at its raw GitHub source 2026-08-23) grounds its central claim in Guo et al. 2017 on neural-network calibration, asserting that because image classifiers are overconfident, coding agents overclaim completion. That inference does not hold: a calibration statistic over a classifier's probability estimates is a different object from an agent's judgment that a multi-step software task is finished. This course grounds the same mechanism in first-party observation of coding agents on real multi-step builds (S1, S5) plus peer-reviewed work on agents and patches specifically (S2, S3, S4, S6), and Lesson 1 includes a short section stating explicitly why the calibration framing is not used and what it fails to yield — three named repairs follow from the observed patterns, none of which follows from 'the model is overconfident'. The competitor also presents its three-layer check as two mermaid diagrams and a CLAUDE.md snippet with no runnable artifact; this course ships a done-condition file format, a gate script, a trigger, an unchecked list, and a terminal exercise that requires overturning a real claim.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: One mermaid diagram in the whole course, in Lesson 6, showing the Stop-hook loop: the agent judging itself complete, the gate running, a failing condition producing a block whose reason is the Lesson 5 failure message, the agent continuing from the named fault, and a dotted edge for the 8-consecutive-block override. It earns its place because the control flow is genuinely circular with a bounded escape, which reads poorly as prose — and the bound is the detail readers most often miss. Lessons 1-5 deliberately use tables instead: the three early-completion patterns, the four blind spots of a green suite, the cost/capability ladder, and the four elements of a repair-ready failure are all classifications rather than flows, and a table shows a classification better than a box diagram. The one place a diagram was considered and rejected is the three-layer ladder in Lesson 4 — the competitor draws exactly that as a left-to-right flowchart, and it conveys strictly less than the table does, which additionally carries what each layer cannot catch and what it costs.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the design brief — six lessons against six named themes — and was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run. No human reviewed the lesson order, the coverage, or the depth before the prose was written. The DAG and load checks were run mechanically and passed, but the judgment that these six themes in this order are what this reader needs rests entirely on the brief.

Lesson 6's hook material is the most perishable content in the course. Event names, decision field names, and the 8-consecutive-block bound are product surface documented for one harness at one version. The lesson carries an explicit warning and teaches the mechanism as the durable part, but a reader following the shape of the example against a changed API will still hit friction, and the example is not runnable as written against any other harness.

The gate script in Lesson 6 is bash with npm commands. A reader on Python, Go, Rust, or a monorepo has to translate before doing anything, and the course states the substitution rule in prose rather than providing a language-neutral version. This is the single largest barrier to the terminal task actually being completed by a reader whose stack differs.

Every quantitative claim in the course comes from a benchmark or survey setting, not from the reader's project, and several are wide (ImpossibleBench cheating rates spanning 2.9% to 76% by suite and 1% to above 85% by prompt). Each carries its setting and an upper-bound-versus-typical note in prose, but a reader who skims will still come away with numbers that do not transfer, and the density of caveats may read as hedging.

The course asserts that layer 3 is where failures survive, on the strength of METR's measured grader-versus-maintainer gap plus Anthropic's end-to-end observation. Neither source measured a three-layer gate of the kind this course builds, and no source prescribes three layers. The ladder is declared a synthesis in Lesson 4's prose, and it remains an untested arrangement of separately-evidenced parts.

No lesson teaches the reader to write the underlying tests or the drive-conditions script, both of which Lesson 6 assumes exist as files. A reader with no layer 2 or layer 3 today can complete a reduced version of the terminal task (the lesson offers an honest minimum), but the full gate requires scripting the course does not teach.

Check whether learn-agent-first-real-task lesson 4 changes; this course's boundary depends on that lesson owning by-hand transcript reading, and the cross-reference in the README and Lesson 1 assumes it.

acceptanceReview.terminalTask: In Lesson 6 the learner installs verify/gate.sh in a repository they actually work in, wires it to a trigger (harness hook, pre-commit, or CI), proves the trigger fires by deliberately breaking a condition and confirming red arrives without them invoking anything, writes verify/UNCHECKED.md naming at least three real uncovered items, and then runs a genuine task through the gate with its done-condition file written before the work — recording the agent's verbatim completion claim, the gate's verdict, and the gap between them. The exercise explicitly requires overturning one real claim, and specifies what to do if three tasks pass cleanly: treat it as a finding about condition strength and rewrite at least one condition, rather than as a pass.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Four blocks across six lessons, all outside the exercise regions, none in Lessons 3 or 6 where the construction work carries the load. Lesson 1, agentmentor-check on what a re-check establishes: serves the misconception that asking 'are you sure?' produces a second opinion, with distractors covering the partial-credit reading ('it rules out careless errors') and the overcorrection ('self-correction reliably degrades') so the reader cannot arrive by eliminating absurdities. Lesson 2, agentmentor-order ranking four green signals: serves the overcorrection that follows the lesson's argument — that if tests are insufficient all checks are equally weak — by forcing the reader to rank on who controls the check and what layer it observes, with the load-bearing distinction being that agent-authored tests rank below an untouched unit suite. Lesson 4, agentmentor-order on the cost ladder: serves the reflex to order by perceived rigour rather than cost, with the two genuinely close calls being the middle pair and the placement of the LLM judge after the browser run. Lesson 5, agentmentor-check on which failure message invites the wrong repair: serves the misconception that a precise mismatch is a good agent-facing message, and its correct answer is deliberately the most professionally-written option, which is the point. Two agentmentor-action cards, in Lessons 1 and 4, plus one in Lesson 6: each is a distinct mode (reasoning_audit on separating beliefs from signals, pressure_scenario on whether layer 3 drives the path where the reader's bugs live, error_simulation on finding loopholes in the reader's own conditions), and each requires the reader to supply their own artifact so the agent cannot re-teach the lesson generically. The judgment interaction the brief required — deciding whether a given 'done' claim should be believed — is the Lesson 1 check, extended by the Lesson 5 check on whether a failure message steers toward a real fix.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets a developer already shipping agent output who distrusts it without a repeatable way to check it — a reader defined by having the problem rather than by lacking the vocabulary. Hidden prerequisites removed: no test framework API is required, since Lessons 1-2 work on the suite the reader already runs and Lesson 4 orders commands they already have; no CI account is required, since the trigger may be a local hook; no browser automation is required, since Lesson 6 states an honest minimum layer 3 of starting the app and performing one request; no harness-specific configuration knowledge is required, since the hook is taught as a mechanism with a warning that syntax is version-specific. The first independent action — sorting one real completion message into reported beliefs and external signals, then checking one belief by hand — uses only reading a message the learner already has plus one command or file open, both in knownConcepts, and it is the same operation the whole course scales up. Nothing in the ramp depends on an unknownConcept: the done-condition file in Lesson 3 is hand-written JSON with no tooling, and automation arrives only in Lesson 6 after three lessons of building the artifact it automates.
promotionNotes: Before any promotion to examples/, re-open S9 (Claude Code hooks) and confirm the Stop event, the decision/reason fields, and the 8-consecutive-block bound are unchanged. This is the course's most version-sensitive content and it sits in the terminal lesson.

Consider adding a language-neutral gate skeleton to Lesson 6 alongside the bash/npm one. The current script is one concrete instance and a non-JavaScript reader must translate before starting the terminal task — the most likely point of abandonment.

The outline was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run. Have a target reader review lesson order and depth before this is treated as a reference course; the DAG is mechanically sound but no human judged the fit.
